title: Seattle Times and Newsday are the latest publications to sue OpenAI and Microsoft
content:
Two more news organizations are suing OpenAI and Microsoft over the supposed use of their journalism to train AI.
A lawsuit filed by The Seattle Times and Newsday argued that with the advent of AI, the journalism industry could become “broken beyond repair.” The lawsuit described generative AI as “a snake eating its own tail” that could “destroy the very organizations” that produce the content it’s trained on.
“AI products like ChatGPT and CoPilot are touted as producers of content, but in fact they are rapacious consumers, devouring human-authored content and delivering back to the world copies and derivative imitations of that same original content they consumed to achieve their commercial objectives,” the lawsuit said.
Back in 2023, The New York Times sued OpenAI and its partner/investor Microsoft over alleged copyright infringement; other publications have followed suit as the case continued. The Seattle Times’ lawsuit is particularly notable because Microsoft and OpenAI have funded some of the organization’s journalism projects and fellowships.
A Microsoft spokesperson told GeekWire that the company is “surprised by the lawsuit” but is “always happy to sit down and explore solutions to this type of dispute.”

report.summary: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming AI training uses their journalism unfairly and could destroy news organizations.
report.background: This lawsuit is part of a wave of litigation against AI companies by news publishers. The New York Times launched a landmark copyright case against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, and several other outlets have since filed similar suits over the unlicensed use of their articles to train generative AI models. The new suit, filed by The Seattle Times and Newsday, argues that AI systems like ChatGPT and Copilot consume human-authored journalism and return derivative imitations, threatening the economic foundation of the news industry. What makes this case stand out is that Microsoft and OpenAI had previously funded Seattle Times journalism projects and fellowships, adding a layer of complexity to the dispute. Microsoft responded that it was surprised by the lawsuit and open to dialogue.
key_points: The lawsuit accuses OpenAI and Microsoft of treating news articles as raw material for AI training. It argues that ChatGPT and Copilot are not true content creators but 'rapacious consumers' that copy and imitate original journalism, undermining the publications that produce it.

This action follows the New York Times' 2023 copyright lawsuit and similar cases from other publishers. The plaintiffs seek accountability for what they see as systematic, unauthorized use of copyrighted news content to build commercial AI products.

The Seattle Times' unique relationship with OpenAI and Microsoft makes the case notable. The tech companies had financially supported the paper's journalism projects and fellowships, meaning the lawsuit highlights a breakdown in what had previously been a collaborative relationship.

The lawsuit warns that AI could leave journalism 'broken beyond repair.' Because AI models depend on human-authored content for training, the legal filing calls it 'a snake eating its own tail' that could eliminate the very organizations producing reliable news.

Microsoft responded with a measured tone, expressing surprise at the lawsuit while stating a willingness to 'sit down and explore solutions.' This suggests neither side is completely closing the door on a negotiated settlement, but the legal battle is already underway.
report.impact: This lawsuit adds momentum to a broader legal push that could reshape how AI companies obtain training data. If the plaintiffs succeed, OpenAI and Microsoft may need to secure explicit licenses from publishers, pay retroactive compensation, or alter how their models process copyrighted text. That would increase costs and could slow development of large language models. For developers, the case signals a need to review data-sourcing practices and invest in licensed or synthetic datasets. For everyday users, the outcome may affect whether news summaries and citations remain freely available in chatbots, or become restricted behind paid partnerships. The ruling could also set a precedent for other creative industries, making this a pivotal moment for AI copyright law.
report.tools: To track this and similar copyright cases, CourtListener (an open-source legal research platform) offers free docket access. Those interested in AI transparency can also review OpenAI's model documentation and Microsoft's responsible AI resources, which discuss training data and content policies. Publications like TechCrunch and GeekWire provide ongoing coverage.
